title: Calendar Days Apart
statement:
You get two valid dates a and b written as "YYYY-MM-DD" in the Gregorian calendar. Return how many days apart they are, as a non-negative number.

A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100, which are leap years only if they are also divisible by 400. Do not use a built-in date library; the point is to do the arithmetic yourself.

examples.why: 2024 is a leap year, so February 29 sits in between.
2100 is divisible by 4 but also by 100 and not by 400, so it is not a leap year.
The order of the dates does not matter, and the gap crosses a year boundary.

constraints: Both dates are valid and between 1971-01-01 and 2100-12-31
hints: Comparing two dates directly is messy. Is there a single number you could compute for each date?
Turn each date into the number of days since a fixed starting point, then subtract.
Days since 1971-01-01: add 365 or 366 for each full year before, then the lengths of the full months before in this year (February is 29 in a leap year), then the day of the month.

explain.intuition:
Dates are a mixed-radix number: days roll into months of uneven length, months into years of 365 or 366 days. Subtracting two such numbers digit by digit is error-prone. The standard fix is to convert each date to a plain day count from one fixed origin, then subtract the two counts. It is the same idea as a Unix timestamp, just in days.

The only real rule to get right is the leap year: divisible by 4, but century years only when divisible by 400. So 2000 is a leap year and 2100 is not.
steps: For a date, start from 0 and add 365 or 366 for every year from 1971 up to the year before.
Add the lengths of the months before the date's month, using 29 for February in a leap year.
Add the day of the month.
Return the absolute difference of the two counts.
pitfalls: Treating every year divisible by 4 as a leap year. 2100 is not.
Adding the current month's length instead of only the full months before it.
Returning a negative number when the first date is later.

complexity.time: O(years in range) per date, effectively O(1)

solutions.title: Step one day at a time
solutions.idea: Start at the earlier date and advance a day at a time, rolling the month and year over, until you reach the later date.

solutions.title: Day number from a fixed origin
solutions.idea: Map each date to the count of days since 1971-01-01 (full years, then full months, then days) and subtract.

followups: Return the weekday of a date, given that 1971-01-01 was a Friday.
Remove the year range limit. How do you count leap years before year y in O(1)?
lcTitle: Number of Days Between Two Dates
